questions.q: Why does the lesson say the single-pilot-team SRE structure doesn't scale on its own as an organization grows?
options: Because SLOs become mathematically invalid once more than one service uses them

Because once many services want the same kind of support, the structure either duplicates uncoordinated tooling across teams or stays confined to the original pilot team — it has to change deliberately or it fails quietly
Because error budgets can only be calculated for exactly one team at a time
Because postmortems become optional once a company passes a certain headcount
questions.explain: Without a deliberate structural change, the organization either ends up with every team building its own inconsistent SRE tooling, or the practice simply never spreads past the original pilot team.

questions.q: What is the real advantage of the embedded SRE model, and what does it trade away for that advantage?
options: Advantage: lower total headcount cost. Trade-off: no on-call coverage at all
Advantage: company-wide consistency. Trade-off: slower incident response

Advantage: deep, specific context on one service's failure modes and history. Trade-off: breadth and leverage — practices and tooling tend to diverge across teams, and the SRE can drift into being just an extra ops hand
Advantage: eliminates the need for SLOs entirely. Trade-off: higher cloud costs
questions.explain: An embedded SRE gains deep service-specific knowledge from living inside one team, but that depth comes at the cost of consistency and leverage across the organization, and a real risk of sliding into a generic ops role.

questions.q: What is the real advantage of a centralized SRE org, and what does it trade away for that advantage?
options: Advantage: shared tooling and standards built once and applied across many teams. Trade-off: distance — losing close, service-specific context, and risking being seen as an outside auditor rather than a partner
Advantage: every engineer in the company becomes an SRE automatically
Advantage: eliminates the need for postmortems. Trade-off: higher latency on every service
Advantage: guarantees 100% uptime across all services. Trade-off: higher headcount cost than the embedded model
questions.explain: Centralizing SRE gets leverage — one dashboard, one incident process, one postmortem standard built once — but it can lose the close context an embedded SRE has, and can feel like an outside audit rather than a true partnership.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why do most organizations that scale SRE well end up with a hybrid model rather than a pure embedded or pure centralized structure?
options: A hybrid model is required by most compliance frameworks
Pure models are always illegal for any publicly traded company
Hybrid models cost exactly half as much as either pure model

It matches each part of the practice to the structure that actually serves it — central leverage for shared infrastructure, proximity for service-specific judgment — rather than being a compromise born of indecision
questions.explain: The hybrid approach is a deliberate design choice: a central team builds and maintains shared platform tooling and standards, while product-aligned or rotating SRE presence applies it to each service's actual operational reality.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say self-service SRE tooling becomes necessary, not optional, as service count grows?
options: Linear headcount growth with service count doesn't work past a certain scale, so letting a team define its own SLO through a standard platform frees the limited central or embedded SRE capacity for genuinely hard problems
Self-service tooling is only useful for marketing purposes, not for operations
Self-service tooling eliminates the need for error budgets entirely
Self-service tooling is required only for services with fewer than ten users
questions.explain: Once the number of services outpaces how fast SRE headcount can realistically grow, self-service tooling lets teams operate their own SLOs without a dedicated SRE for every service, freeing scarce expert capacity for harder problems.
